text:
Every Indian needs to know about this because it is a massive deal for how we trust anything on the internet.

Let me explain.

When you open your bank's website, there's a small padlock next to the web address. That padlock means two things. 

First, that you're talking to your real bank. 

And second that nobody can read what you type, like your password.

So how does your browser know the website is real?

It checks the website's certificate. Think of it like an ID card for a website. 

Your Aadhaar is trusted because the government issued it. A website's ID card is trusted because a certificate authority issued it.

A certificate authority, or CA, is a company that browsers like Chrome, Firefox and Safari already trust. If a CA says "yes, this really is this bank's website," your browser believes it and shows the padlock.

eMudhra is an Indian CA. It's a big one, with more than 60 million certificates issued over the years.

So how does a CA sign these ID cards?

Every CA has a secret number called a private key. It uses that number to put a stamp on each certificate. 

Your browser checks the stamp to confirm it really came from that CA.

The whole system only works if that number is impossible to guess. 

For the type of key in this story, it's supposed to be around 116 digits long. 

Every computer on Earth working together for billions of years wouldn't be able to guess a number like that, just because of the sheer combinations that exist.

But here's what happened.

On October 17, Mozilla got a report that the private keys behind eight eMudhra certificates had been compromised. 

The report came through a person called Wayne on Google's Chrome team.

The keys weren't 116 digits long. 

All eight keys were smaller than 256. Security researcher Scott Helme found that one of them was just the number 4. Others were 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

So anyone could break them by trying 256 numbers. A basic laptop does that in less than a second.

Mozilla didn't need to know how Wayne did it. Its own team recovered the keys within two hours. Since then, several other people have found them on their own too.

To understand the gravity of the problem, a bad actor could make fake ID cards for any website they want. 

Your bank, your email, a government portal. 

Browsers that trusted eMudhra would have checked the fake stamp and shown the padlock like everything was fine.

If someone could get between you and the internet, say on public Wi-Fi, they could show you a fake site with a real-looking padlock and read or change what you send.

eMudhra says a script used during its key creation process back in April 2025 had a flaw. It made a second, much weaker set of keys, and those were used by mistake to create the certificates.

That means these weak keys were there for about a year and a half before anyone caught it. eMudhra says the person who found it may have used AI-assisted techniques.

The good news is that the response was fast.

Mozilla received the report at 8:06 pm UTC on October 17 and had pushed a block to Firefox users by 10:59 pm.

Google, Apple and Microsoft have also blocked these certificates for their users. 

eMudhra revoked all eight the next morning and stopped issuing new certificates from the affected root. 

Mozilla is now removing that root certificate from Firefox's trusted list altogether.

But there's still a lot of clean-up to do.

Browsers are mostly covered. But plenty of apps, servers and backend systems don't check these block lists. They need software updates to stop trusting the bad certificates, and some of those updates are still pending.

Real websites that used eMudhra are also affected. Yash Kadakia, founder of Security Brigade, estimates around 30,000 legitimate certificates will need to be moved over. A lot of those are likely Indian businesses and services.

See, we're moving our whole lives online, UPI, banking, tax filing, DigiLocker, government services. 

All of it rests on this invisible layer of trust.

So, when an Indian company that's trusted by every major browser makes a mistake this basic, it hurts how the world sees Indian digital infrastructure.

This has happened before, and it went very badly. 

In 2011, a Dutch CA called DigiNotar was hacked, and fake Google certificates were used to spy on people in Iran. 

Browsers stopped trusting it completely, and the company shut down soon after.

For now, here's what you can do. Keep your browser and apps updated on your phone and laptop. 

Be careful on public Wi-Fi. Type your bank's website address yourself instead of clicking links.

eMudhra still owes India a clear, public explanation of how a key that protects millions of people ended up being the number 4.

text: @grok @Nostre_damus Why this post is withheld in India?

The post quotes Polymarket, whose entire X account is currently withheld in India in response to a legal demand. This stems from Indian government orders under the IT Act (Section 69A) and the 2025 Online Gaming Act, which classify prediction markets as prohibited online money games. The content stays visible outside India.

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

Elon Musk restricted Starlink in Ukraine, and an entire military operation went dark.

That wasn't just a corporate decision. It was a warning label for India.

We celebrate UPI. We cheer for our space missions. We talk a lot about digital sovereignty. But peel back the layers, and the reality gets uncomfortable.

Our critical infrastructure is basically renting space on foreign-controlled tech.

Here is the actual ground reality:
- We built NavIC for navigation. But with only three active satellites right now, we still lean heavily on the US GPS system.

- We have our own government cloud. Yet, thousands of Indian institutions are fundamentally tied to AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

- UPI broke the Visa and Mastercard monopoly. But the consumer apps running the show? Dominated by Google Pay and PhonePe.

Even our indigenous Tejas fighter jets rely on American-made GE Aerospace engines.

Building the front-end application is a great first step. 

But true autonomy means owning the underlying stack.

In a global crisis, whoever controls the servers, the satellites, and the supply chains holds the ultimate leverage.

We built a beautiful house. It is time we bought the land underneath it.

text: Eight digital certificates issued by eMudhra had weak secret keys that researchers said could be cracked in under a second. They could potentially have been used to impersonate trusted websites or sign malicious software. https://t.co/xBXlgOYVDw
Google, Apple, Microsoft and Mozilla have blocked the affected certificates, while India’s IT Ministry says digital signature and eSign services remain unaffected. https://t.co/o8NrxGUaab

One of the simplest ways for a government or large authority to restrict access to certain websites across a region is DNS-level blocking through ISP resolvers. In India, this is exactly how most website restrictions are enforced. By default, your device relies on the ISP’s DNS resolver, so DNS-based blocking takes effect automatically. However, this can often be bypassed by switching to third-party DNS resolvers such as Cloudflare(1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8).

Compared to this, China is much stricter, as China deploys censorship at multiple network layers simultaneously, making circumvention exponentially harder.

China’s Great Firewall works by checking internet traffic at many different levels, not just DNS. It uses Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) to look inside data packets as they travel through the network. It performs SNI inspection to read the domain name you’re trying to reach during the HTTPS handshake, which is why simply switching DNS doesn’t bypass it.

It also blocks the entire IP ranges of platforms like Google, Facebook, and YouTube at the router level, so even if you obtain the correct IP through a service like Cloudflare DNS, the connection is immediately dropped.

The system carries out active probing, where it tests servers that appear to be VPNs and blocks them quickly if confirmed. Finally, it uses protocol fingerprinting to study traffic patterns such as packet timing and size to detect VPN or proxy traffic even when the data is fully encrypted.

China is highly dedicated to preventing people from using foreign websites and instead pushes them to use their own.

A privacy-first DNS resolver just chose to leave an entire country rather than lie to its users.

Quad9 is shutting off its free DNS service in France on November 24, after a French court ordered it to block domains that BeIN Sports claimed were facilitating sports piracy.

Quad9 refused.

"We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations."

The court had actually reduced the fine to just €1,000 per day. Quad9 still walked away. Because the real problem was not the fine. It was the precedent.

Complying would mean either applying French copyright law to Quad9's global DNS infrastructure, or using geo-blocking methods that Quad9 considers technically unreliable and ethically compromised. Either way, the integrity of the service breaks.

This is what it looks like when a privacy tool takes its mission seriously. Most services would have quietly blocked the domains and moved on. Quad9 chose to exit instead 👏

In April of 2025, eMudhra (an Indian Certificate Authority), published 8 intermediate CA keys which were so weak that a small child could guess the numbers in a few seconds.

One of the private keys was, literally, 4.

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

SUPPORTING REPORTING

2. The Indian Express — Background on Sahyog and the growth of government-directed takedowns: https://t.co/vYXKHDlsAU

Source: The Indian Express Hindi — video explainer based on reporting by Soumyarendra Barik.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

In an important development for freedom of expression and digital rights, the Punjab and Haryana High Court has reportedly held that social media users whose content is targeted for blocking must receive a copy of the government's intimation sent to the intermediary, immediately after it is issued.

This is a significant affirmation of a fundamental democratic principle: **The government cannot exercise censorship powers without procedural fairness and accountability.**

**WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DEMOCRACY**

Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression, subject to constitutionally permissible restrictions under Article 19(2).

When the government seeks to block a citizen's social media content, that citizen should have a meaningful opportunity to understand the grounds for the action and pursue an appropriate legal remedy.

The principles of natural justice demand transparency, fairness and protection against arbitrary executive action.

**FIVE QUESTIONS EVERY CITIZEN SHOULD ASK**

1. Why should a citizen discover that their content has been blocked without knowing the government's reasons?

2. How can someone challenge censorship if the government withholds the communication underlying the blocking action?

3. Should social media intermediaries be allowed to implement government blocking directions without adequate procedural safeguards for affected users?

4. Who ensures that blocking powers are not misused to suppress criticism, dissent or legitimate political opposition?

5. If government action is lawful and justified, why should procedural transparency be feared?

**NATIONAL SECURITY CANNOT BECOME A BLANKET EXCUSE FOR ARBITRARY CENSORSHIP.**

Legitimate restrictions may sometimes be necessary under the Constitution. But every restriction must satisfy applicable legal requirements, and safeguards must prevent disproportionate interference with fundamental rights.

This reported ruling is particularly relevant to independent journalists, activists, opposition voices, whistleblowers and ordinary citizens who rely on social media to participate in democratic debate.

**OUR DEMAND**

Every government-initiated content-blocking process must respect constitutional protections, applicable disclosure requirements, due process and meaningful access to judicial review.

The right to criticise the government is not a favour granted by those in power. It is an essential part of constitutional democracy.

**A DEMOCRACY THAT SILENCES QUESTIONS WEAKENS ITSELF. A DEMOCRACY THAT PROTECTS DISSENT STRENGTHENS ITS CONSTITUTION.**

the internet just hit the panic button.

hundreds of millions of websites could be wide open to hackers right now.

governments, banks and major platforms are pulling their own sites offline to stay safe.

people are already calling it "black october."

and the cause is something you've probably never heard of but use every single day.

php. the code behind roughly 7 in 10 websites.

two critical bugs, nicknamed php2shell, let attackers walk in without ever needing a password. both scored 9.2 out of 10 on severity.

details started spreading on oct 20. emergency fixes landed the next day. by then, hackers were already inside the gates.

cloudflare's ceo says attack attempts exploded from thousands to millions in just hours.

security agencies in several countries are giving php site owners one order: patch it now or take it down.

sites have gone dark all over the world, from government portals and hospitals to banks.

crowdstrike says these attacks barely leave a trace, so some sites may already be hit and have no clue.

the numbers are wild:

- around 2.6 million public servers run php, each possibly hosting hundreds of sites
- over 1.1 million are on old versions that no longer get official updates

those older setups need an upgrade to a supported version or a fix from their provider.

and even a patch won't remove a backdoor a hacker may have already planted.

cloudflare also says attackers are now reshaping their attacks to sneak past its defenses.

but php isn't the only fire burning right now:

- japan's onamae shut down every desktop cloud plan after malware showed up on customer servers
- india's emudhra had 8 certificate keys so weak, one of them was literally the number "4"
- state bank of india confirmed 3,897 customer records on the dark web
- criminals used ai agents to break into 400+ latin american banks
- capcom confirmed a breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses
- gitlab revealed a 10/10 severity flaw in versions going back to 2014
- litellm pulled a release that contained malware, and railway flagged possible exposure of customer secrets

none of these has a confirmed link to php2shell.

it's a pile of separate breaches all landing at once.

the real number of incidents could take months to come out.

the world is still on high alert. and the attacks aren't done yet. https://t.co/4a4XkIisk7

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

text:
South Korean police just busted the largest illegal gambling case in the country's history: $17.3 billion in wagers across 188 websites.

The operation ran from March 2023 to July 2026, directed from bases in Vietnam and Cambodia. The model split into two layers: suppliers secured casino video feeds and credits from legit overseas gaming companies, then handed that off to developers (one previously at a major Korean conglomerate) who built software that could launch a fully working gambling site in about 10 minutes.

Site operators paid $1,100-$2,200/month for maintenance, a subscription model that scaled the network to 188 properties without each one needing its own tech team.

77 arrested (25 suppliers, 33 operators, 19 players), $7.2M in assets frozen, 118 sites shut down plus 408 blocked addresses. 12 suspects still overseas, Interpol Red Notices in motion.

One official's quote says it all: they're now targeting the supply chain itself, not just playing whack-a-mole with individual sites.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
My problem with constitutional adjudication in general is how easily the Supreme Court gets pulled into deciding questions with no facts behind them. People file petitions under Article 32 on facts that are never proved and ask the Court to test government action against them. 

To be clear, yes a writ lies for an actual or anticipated violation of a fundamental right. But “anticipated” still has to mean something. There has to be a real person facing a real prospect of the right being taken away, not a possibility someone has imagined sitting inside a lawyer’s office.

Take this case. We don't know if the petitioner was ever compelled to do this. We don't know if he’s going to attend an event where he’ll be compelled to. We don’t know whether his religious belief is sincerely held or how central it is to his practice. There isn’t a single actual instance where the right was violated.

These are not technicalities. A free exercise claim under Article 25 turns on facts which may look like this: what the belief is, how it’s practised, what exactly the State is making the person do, and whether that falls within public order, morality or health. Every one of those is a factual question. 

You can’t answer them on a set of assumptions in a petition. And the Supreme Court sitting under Article 32 is not a trial court. There’s no evidence led, no cross-examination, nothing whatsoever is tested. It decides on affidavits. When the affidavits themselves rest on hypotheticals, the State is left defending its action in the abstract, and the Court ends up laying down law that binds all future courts and everyone under Article 141 on a record that tells it almost nothing.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

The Delhi High Court has reserved its verdict on Telegram's challenge to the Centre's temporary blocking order. The Centre argued that Telegram's bots and mirror channels allow illegal content to reappear within minutes, while Telegram said it already uses AI and hash-based tools to detect and remove such content.

The case could redefine the limits of platform regulation, free communication, and intermediary liability in India.

🇺🇸 Investing in US Stocks from India? Some key points to consider. 🇮🇳

Many platforms offer access to US stocks such as Nvidia, Apple and Tesla nowadays.

Before investing, understand the costs, compliance requirements and risks 👇

⚠️ 1. Currency Risk

A stock can rise in USD while rupee appreciation reduces your INR return.

FX spreads and conversion charges also affect returns. Costs vary by provider and transaction.

⚠️ 2. RBI / LRS Rules

Overseas investments must comply with applicable Indian foreign-exchange rules.

Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, the annual limit is currently USD 250,000 per individual, subject to regulations and exclusions.

Confirm that the investment and remittance route are permitted before transferring funds.

⚠️ 3. TCS & Cash Flow

Tax collected at source (TCS) may apply to certain LRS remittances after the applicable threshold.

It is generally available as a credit against tax liability, subject to applicable rules and reporting, but may temporarily reduce cash flow.

Rates and thresholds depend on the remittance’s nature and purpose and may change. Verify the current position before remitting.

⚠️ 4. Tax Complexity

Foreign shares may require:

- Capital-gains calculations
- Dividend reporting
- Foreign-asset disclosures in your Indian income-tax return, where applicable

Holding-period rules, tax rates and reporting requirements may differ from those for Indian securities.

Keep transaction, exchange-rate and tax records.

⚠️ 5. Broker & Custody Risk

Shares may be held through:

- A US broker
- An Indian intermediary
- A custodian
- Another structure

Investor protection, asset segregation, complaint mechanisms and coverage limits depend on the entities and applicable laws.

Read the account and custody documents carefully.

⚠️ 6. Dividend Tax

US dividends may face US withholding tax.

A reduced treaty rate may be available only if required conditions and documentation are met. Rates are not automatically the same for every investor or platform.

Foreign-tax-credit relief in India may also be available, subject to eligibility, limits and compliance.

⚠️ 7. Estate-Tax Exposure

Direct ownership of US-situs assets can create US estate-tax filing or tax considerations for non-US residents, including Indian residents.

The implications may depend on:

- Asset value
- Ownership structure
- Applicable law

Treaty provisions, exemptions and filing thresholds may matter even when no tax is ultimately payable.

Obtain specialist advice as portfolios grow.

⚠️ 8. Trading Limitations

Platforms may not support:

- Fractional-share transfers
- Advanced orders
- Every investment strategy

US derivatives and leveraged products may create separate regulatory, suitability and tax issues for Indian residents.

💡 The Big Takeaway

Zero brokerage doesn't mean zero cost.

Your net return can be affected by:

- Currency conversion charges
- Taxes that temporarily reduce liquidity
- Custody arrangements
- Account fees
- Withdrawal charges

Before choosing a platform, compare the total cost, legal ownership, regulatory compliance and exit process — not just the sign-up offer. Think as investors bafter 5yrs. 

US market access is an opportunity. Understanding the fine print is risk management.

Disclaimer: Rules, tax rates, thresholds, reporting requirements and broker protections can change. Verify current details with qualified tax, legal and financial professionals before investing or remitting funds.

But there is no FDA inspection. We have no idea what they're getting. There's no way for them to know what they're getting. And so our objective was Americans are going to be buying these anyway. Our objective was to make sure that there is a regulated marketplace so that what they're getting is what they claim to be, that it's safe, that the factories are inspected. And this is a market that we had before, before the Biden administration, in a very, very aggressive, over- overreach, just made a decision to get rid of all peptides. That is not what the Supreme Court said. 

You know, the drug— FDA has the authority to regulate drugs under certain conditions. It has the authority to regulate drugs if they may, if they're mass marketed and they make a specific claim about a specific indication, like we're going to cure cancer or whatever. But if it's a— but most Dietary supplements and most remedies are not regulated in that way. There is no nutritional supplements. You can go in a drugstore and buy nutritional supplements. None of those have ever been subjected to double-blind placebo-controlled trials, which are very expensive, billion dollars. And there's also 30% of the prescriptions that are written in this country are for off-label uses. So that drug has never been tested for that indication. And the rule is generally that FDA should regulate it if there's a safety signal. But if there's no safety signal, it's between you and your doctor, as long as it's not mass marketed and as long as it doesn't claim a specific indication.

The Bombay High Court on Friday struck down the amendments to Information Technology (IT) Rules allowing the Central government to establish Fact-Check Units. 

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB). 

Under the new rules, if the fact check unit comes across or is informed about any posts that are “fake”, “false” or contain “misleading” facts pertaining to the business of the government, it would flag it to the social media intermediaries.

The online intermediaries would then have to take down such content if they wanted to retain their “safe harbour” (legal immunity against third-party content).

The state’s closing argument went after Meta for ending its third-party fact-checking program. “𝘉𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘣𝘰𝘥𝘺 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘵-𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘤𝘬𝘦𝘥, 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘶𝘭𝘢𝘳𝘭𝘺 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳, 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘋𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘥 𝘛𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘺 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘢 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦…𝘍𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘣𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘦’𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘳𝘪𝘥 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘵-𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘤𝘬 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘮,” the state told jurors, in favor of community notes.

The Free Beacon says the state never showed the statements caused harm to anyone, or that any New Mexico resident had even heard them. The order also carries 15 percent annual interest, or $𝟑.𝟕𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫, against a state budget of $11.1 billion.

Meta will appeal. Chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said the case “𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘬𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘢 𝘵𝘢𝘹 𝘰𝘯 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘦𝘤𝘩 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘯𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘤𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘸 𝘳𝘶𝘭𝘦𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘴𝘢𝘺 𝘰𝘯𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘦.” For now, the largest judgment of its kind belongs to a prosecutor who once prosecuted fewer than half of Albuquerque’s violent crimes, according to the Free Beacon.

Deliberately tried the same tasks tonight in Grok @bot and @ChatGPT Dots. Based on everything I've been seeing on X lately, my results were not as expected:

Task 1 Prompt: Check my voter registration and register for mail-in application since I'll be out of town on election day.

Grok Bot: Requested my driver's license # and DOB even though that info is already available in my 2nd brain. Successfully confirmed I am already registered to vote. Got stuck on a captcha when trying to request a mail-in ballot. After my captcha completion, it successfully completed the request and submitted it.

Dot: Didn't ask for any additional ID info, confirmed my voter registration status. Went through to end of the mail-in request, asked me to confirm. I stopped it at this final step because Grok already submitted my request.

Winner Task 1: Dot

Task 2 Prompt: Order me on Amazon the same bar of soap that I've ordered a few times in the last couple months.

Grok Bot: Checked my emails for recent soap purchases - found one from 2025, but not the one I've ordered recently. After me saying that was wrong it opened Amazon, found my recent orders, went to the checkout page, and then got stopped by Amazon's AI Agent blocker and said it can't go any further.

Dot: Initially tried it's cloud browser, but got hit with AI blocker nearly instantly while looking in recent history. Switched to Chrome, found the correct soap, put it in cart, asked for final confirmation. I said "approved" and it placed the order successfully.

Winner Task 2: Dot

These are obviously 2 very specific requests, but I stand by the fact that ChatGPT Dots' ability to initiate Computer Use or Chrome, make it much less likely to leave tasks unfinished.

Yes it is absolutely true that Dots guardrails will have it stop more frequently asking for permission, but when granted permission it is much more capable to completing any given task.
